items.title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
items.raw_text: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. items.title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
items.raw_text: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs. The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. items.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
items.raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.raw_text: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. Google Scholar, library catalogues and generative AI are part of their everyday research routines. But what role do traditional subject-specific databases still play? These questions are at the heart of our new study (in German) „Zwischen Google Scholar und ChatGPT – Wie Wirtschaftsstudierende heute recherchieren“ (“Between Google Scholar and ChatGPT – How economics and business students conduct research today”). Between March and May 2026, we conducted an online survey of 908 economics and business students at German universities. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. items.raw_text: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2. In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off. As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed. Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. items.title: In Memoriam: Jan-Ewout van der Putten
items.raw_text: Op 30 september 2026 overleed Jan-Ewout van der Putten, 78 jaar oud. Hij was tien jaar plaatsvervangend griffier van de Eerste Kamer geweest en vervolgens zes jaar wethouder voor D66 in Den Haag. Zijn directeurschap viel samen met een ingrijpende periode van bibliotheekvernieuwing. Van der Putten behoorde tot de landelijke hoofdrolspelers in dat proces. items.title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
items.raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. items.raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. items.raw_text: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. The hacks that didn't have to happen Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update

items.title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation
items.raw_text: Most planetary scientists will tell you the heyday of Venus exploration was more than a generation ago. That is about to change. Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The first, known as the Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), is now scheduled for launch in December 2030, a year earlier than previously planned. DAVINCI will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through the atmosphere of Venus, returning the first direct images of the planet's surface since 1982. A second mission, Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS), will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit. The European Space Agency is building another orbiter, Envision, for launch to Venus in 2032. The Venus armada might get started as soon as next year, when Rocket Lab aims to launch a privately funded probe to search for signs of organic material in the planet's clouds. Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
items.raw_text: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. items.title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
items.raw_text: Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread. The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative . Her book, titled Undersea War , explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards like storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly. items.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
items.raw_text: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

items.title: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
items.raw_text: About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way. One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely. I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API. There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues

items.title: Consumentenbond start rechtszaak tegen Meta om camerabril
items.raw_text: De Consumentenbond stapt naar de rechter omdat Meta weigert zijn camerabril aan te passen. De Consumentenbond vroeg om aanpassingen omdat Meta met de bril de privacywet schendt. De zitting is op 26 november 2026 bij de rechtbank Amsterdam. De camerabril kan ongemerkt omstanders filmen, zonder hun toestemming. De beelden die de bril vastlegt, kunnen veel zeggen over de mensen die gefilmd worden. Bijvoorbeeld over hun politieke opvatting, religie en gezondheid. Dit zijn bijzondere persoonsgegevens die niet zomaar mogen worden verwerkt. Ook worden beelden van kinderen vastgelegd met de bril. De gemaakte beelden en geluidsfragmenten kunnen door Meta gebruikt worden voor het trainen van hun AI-modellen. ‘Aanpassing bril of verbod’ De Consumentenbond eist dat Meta de bril en de standaardinstellingen zo verandert dat die voldoet aan de privacywetgeving. Ook moet Meta stoppen met de onrechtmatige verwerking van gegevens voor AI. Wanneer de rechter de Consumentenbond gelijk geeft, moet Meta de aanpassingen binnen 2 weken doorvoeren. Als het volgens Meta niet mogelijk is om de bril aan de wet te laten voldoen, dan wil de Consumentenbond een verbod op de verkoop van de camerabril. Blinden en slechtzienden Consumenten die blind of slechtziend zijn, kunnen baat hebben bij het gebruik van een AI-bril. items.title: EDAY: de toekomst van media inkoop
items.raw_text: De inkoop van digitale campagnes verandert snel: adverteerders zoeken flexibiliteit, snelheid en controle, passend bij hun eigen werkwijze. Met het nieuwe platform Serve speelt Mediahuis hierop in door directe inkoop, programmatic opties (PMP/PG) en integratie via API en MCP mogelijk te maken. Sander van Gestel presenteert Serve voor het eerst op EDAY en laat zien hoe AI-agents, data en menselijke expertise samen de toekomst van media-inkoop vormen. De manier waarop digitale campagnes worden ingekocht, verandert snel. Adverteerders willen campagnes sneller kunnen starten en bijsturen, zonder concessies te doen aan controle, inzicht of persoonlijk advies. Tegelijkertijd verschillen hun wensen sterk. Waar de één zelfstandig een campagne wil opzetten, koopt de ander liever in via bestaande programmatic kanalen of vanuit de eigen systemen. Dat roept een relevante vraag op: hoe ontwerp je een advertentieplatform dat niet iedereen in hetzelfde proces dwingt, maar zich aanpast aan verschillende werkwijzen? En welke rol spelen automatisering, AI en menselijke expertise daarin? Mediahuis onderzocht deze vragen bij de ontwikkeling van Serve, een nieuw platform dat in 2027 wordt gelanceerd. items.title: Cross-border verkoop drijft groei Europese marketplaces
items.raw_text: De honderd grootste online marketplaces die in Europa actief zijn, realiseren dit jaar zo’n 175 miljard aan bruto handelsvolume (GMV). Bijna acht op de tien euro daarvan, 140 miljard, komt uit cross-border transacties. Dat blijkt uit een rapport over de Europese top 100 van marketplaces door CBCommerce . In 2027 zou de totale GMV met ongeveer acht procent kunnen groeien tot 190 miljard euro. Als drijvende krachten achter die groei noemt het rapport AI-gestuurde productontdekking, internationale expansie van de platforms en toenemende investeringen in lokale fulfilmentinfrastructuur in Europa. Internationale platformen breiden hun netwerken van Europese verkopers, magazijnen en bezorgpartners uit, wat de levertijden en betrouwbaarheid ten goede komt. Tegelijkertijd, en dat geldt vooral voor Chinese marktplaatsen, vermijden ze met lokale infrastructuur dat hun klanten invoerheffingen moeten betalen. Aan kop van de ranglijst staan Amazon, Temu en AliExpress, gevolgd door eBay en Etsy. De top 10 bestaat verder uit Vinted, OLX, Zalando, AbeBooks en StockX . De concurrentie blijft hevig. items.raw_text: TomTom kondigt organisatorische veranderingen aan die bedoeld zijn om TomTom doelgerichter, sneller en schaalbaarder te maken. Het bedrijf is opnieuw ingedeeld in drie divisies: Automated Driving (geautomatiseerd rijden), Location Intelligence (locatie-intelligentie) en Navigation (navigatie). Door het aantal managementlagen te verminderen en de besluitvorming dichter bij de uitvoering te brengen, hoopt TomTom sneller op klantbehoeften te reageren en innovatie te versnellen. Hierbij verdwijnen 200 functies. Bij locatie-intelligentie maakt AI het voor klanten eenvoudiger om toegang te krijgen tot locatiegegevens en daar inzichten uit te halen.” Navigatie blijft de ruggengraat van TomTom. Dit is de activiteit waar het grootste deel van de omzet vandaan komt. “De omzet over het derde kwartaal was in lijn met onze verwachtingen, terwijl de operationele marge hoger uitkwam dan verwacht. items.title: Onderzoek invloed AI op digital agencies: tarieven onder druk, eigen data als troef
items.raw_text: De grote reclameholdings bouwen hun verdienmodel om onder druk van AI. WPP verwacht al eventjes dat de tarieven dalen en Monks wil eind 2026 al een kwart van de omzet uit abonnementen halen. Dit en meer blijkt uit een nieuw onderzoek dat Emerce vandaag publiceert. Voor het derde jaar op rij onderzoekt Emerce wat AI doet met digital agencies. Deze keer ligt de nadruk op beursgenoteerde holdings: Dentsu, Monks (S4 Capital), Omnicom/IPG, Publicis Groupe en WPP. Emerce analyseerde hun uitspraken over AI en keek naar wat er werkelijk gebeurde met producten/diensten, omzet, marge en personeel. Zo brengt het in kaart hoe de holdings omgaan met een afbrokkelend urenmodel en tegelijk flinke investeringen in AI. Ook laat het zien wie daarvan profiteert. Publicis groeide in 2025 bijvoorbeeld met 5.900 medewerkers, terwijl WPP, Omnicom/IPG, Dentsu en Monks krompen. Volgens de bestuurders is AI daarbij zelden de belangrijkste reden voor ontslagen: de krimp komt vooral door fusies, reorganisaties en verloren klanten. Daarnaast investeren de holdings fors in eigen klantdata, nu taalmodellen voor iedereen beschikbaar zijn. Die strategie lijkt in pitches al effect te hebben.
